points.en: Doctrinal preaching teaches a basic belief for understanding and acceptance, and evangelistic preaching calls the hearer to decide for Christ.
Pastoral or therapeutic preaching heals by bringing God's comfort to human need, and ethical or prophetic preaching confronts sin and calls to righteous living.
A doctrine is rarely found in one passage but gathered from many texts, and the doctrinal sermon arranges them around one theme, as a topical sermon does.
Topical, textual and expository describe how a sermon is arranged, not how faithful it is, so a topical doctrinal sermon is as biblical as an expository one.
Gives examples, such as the new birth drawn from John, Romans and Peter.
Purpose is the aim, why we preach and what the sermon should accomplish; structure is how the sermon is built, such as topical, textual, expository or narrative.
Gives a coherent example of one purpose carried by a particular structure, such as doctrinal purpose with topical structure.
Notes that structure has little to do with how biblical a sermon is.
Doctrinal preaching begins with a truth or belief, and pastoral preaching often begins with a problem or need such as grief, fear or guilt.
Doctrinal aims at understanding, acceptance and a changed life, while pastoral aims to heal by bringing Scripture to the need.
Notes both must stay rooted in the Word.
Urgency: every hearing of the gospel involves a decision, so the call is to respond today, as in 2 Corinthians 6:2, not someday.
Felix trembled under Paul's reasoning but put off his decision, and it never came, so the evangelist preaches to prevent such delay.
Adds that the sermon should end with a clear, earnest invitation.
The danger is comfort without Christ: borrowed pop-psychology or self-help, advice without the authority of God's Word.
The remedy is to meet the real need but heal with Scripture and keep Christ at the center, rather than merely soothing with sentiment.
Cites Paul comforting grieving believers with the hope of the resurrection, not platitudes.
Nathan confronted a guilty king by telling a story that disarmed David and led him to condemn himself, then named him directly.
Ethical preaching names sin plainly, summons to repentance and marks the road of obedience.
It requires the preacher to be faithful even when the word is unwelcome, willing to confront the powerful.
Notes Nathan's skillful, gracious approach aimed at repentance rather than mere rebuke.
Without grace, ethical preaching becomes moralism or scolding, a list of duties cut off from the gospel.
Righteous living is the glad response of those who have already received God's favor, not a way to earn it.
Law tells us what to do and only the gospel gives the heart to do it, so obedience is pressed on people reminded of God's mercy.
Identifies pastoral or therapeutic preaching as predominant for a grieving, fearful congregation.
Plans to name the loss honestly and bring Scripture to bear on it, comforting with a word from God rather than mere sentiment.
Keeps Christ and the gospel central so the sermon does not become only soothing or self-help.
Cites texts such as Psalm 147:3, Matthew 11:28 or 1 Thessalonians 4:13.
Chooses one Scripture text and shows it preached toward at least three of the four purposes.
Explains how each purpose shapes what is drawn from the text and how it is applied.
Each treatment remains faithful to the passage, with the same text and method serving different aims.
